verdicts.lens:
Physics and interpretation. I read the report body and script, SYNTHESIS.md, the clean-room shirecache_mesh_master.sv and shirecache_pkg.sv, the Shire Cache spec and the NoC bridge list in etsoc_shire_other_esr.h. I did not run anything on the cards. I redid the per-distance analysis from the independent per-burst energies (indep/bursts.json). My scripts are in /tmp/claude-1019/-home-yaroslavvb-claude/ed6d06d5-de26-4323-94f1-0dc808eafbda/scratchpad/verify-hpm/physics/:
- perd.py and perd_v1.py fit the ones/transition model separately at each distance and compare walt against it.
- parity.py tests for a parity or header term.
- share_ab.py, contention.py and load.py relate the extra energy to link sharing and to per-reader bandwidth.

Numbers are fJ per payload bit (per hop where stated). The meter is the mesh (NoC) rail unless board power is named. All reported numbers are reproduced; what does not hold up is several of the physical explanations built on them.

verdicts.claim: C1. Energy per payload byte grows linearly with hop distance for every data pattern. On the mesh rail the data-dependent part is ~0 at d=0 and grows by a constant per hop. Leaving the shire costs about one extra hop.
verdicts.evidence:
d=0 checks out. The per-distance fit (perd.py) gives a transition coefficient of 3-6 fJ/bit and a ones coefficient of 1-2 at d=0, against 299-304 and 84-90 at d=1: about 1-2%. Both independent analyses agree (0.009-0.03 pJ/B).

Linearity is only approximate on the loaded mesh. The d=4 point sits 5-6% above the line for random data and 10-13% for all-ones, where link sharing jumps from 32% to 55%. The link-disjoint set is linear to 0.4-1.3%.

The exit cost is a different kind of cost from a hop, which is why 'about one hop' changes with the pattern:
- Per-distance coefficients for v2 wu, NoC rail, d=1/2/3/4/6: transition term A = 299-304 / 397-406 / 498-505 / 558-570 / 776-795; ones term B = 84-90 / 206-207 / 321-329 / 547-551 / 697-716.
- From d=1 to 3 each hop adds about 98-101 to A and 115-122 to B.
- d=1 already holds about 2 hops' worth of transition energy but less than one hop's worth of ones energy. A straight-line fit gives A = 202-211 + 95·d and B = -50 to -58 + 140·d.
- So the shire crossing charges only for bits that differ from the previous line. All-ones data pay no exit cost: at d=1 all-ones costs 36% less than random (NoC 1.54 vs 2.40 pJ/B, board 5.60 vs 8.95).
- Exit cost in hops is about 0.3 for zeros and 0.5-0.7 for random on the NoC rail, about 1 for random on board power, and about 2 for the 256 B alternating pattern. That pattern's excess is 1.26 pJ/B at d=1 against 0.41 per further hop.
verdicts.required_change: Section 4 should say: 'On the mesh rail the data-dependent energy is zero at d = 0 (under 2% of the one-hop value) and grows by nearly the same amount with each hop. On the loaded mesh the step from 3 to 4 hops is 5-13% larger, where link sharing jumps from 32% to 55%. Leaving the shire costs extra only for bits that differ from the previous line: about one hop for random data on board power, 0.5-0.7 hop on the mesh rail, and nothing for all-ones data.' Replace 'for every data pattern ... the same amount with every hop out to 6' with 'nearly linear'.

verdicts.claim: C2. Per-hop energy depends on the density of ones: all-ones costs about as much as random; P and 1-P differ; the frozen line fits; slope = s0 + a*2P(1-P) + b*P with a = 98 and b = 129 on the NoC rail (board 151/192; v1 95/131 and 139/197); complement test 132 and 129.
verdicts.evidence:
The numbers are reproduced by both independent analyses. NoC-rail a is 97-99 and b is 128-131. The board values agree only with the leakage correction (without it board a is 162).

Checks on the model's assumptions:
- No parity or header toggles on the data wires. Adding a term for 0<P<1 (parity bits toggle about half the time at any density strictly between 0 and 1) to the v1 fit over 7 densities gives -0.4 to -0.5 fJ/bit/hop, and the rms does not change (parity.py).
- 2P(1-P) is the right difference rate between consecutive data flits. In v2 every line is unique. In v1, the flits that follow each other on one lane (lines i and i+4) are always different image lines. v1 and v2 agree: A(d=1) is 297-301 against 299-304, and a is 95 against 98. In v1 the two in-flight loads carry identical lines, so they do not interleave on a lane.
- 'All ones never flips' and 'a one costs more than a flip' are not established. Nothing says the wires hold their value between flit trains. At d=1 each lane carries about 11.7 of an assumed 25.6 GB/s (64 B at 400 MHz), about 46% busy.
- If idle cycles put 0 on the data path (a crossbar output with no grant, or data gated by valid), ordinary static wires give exactly this model. Then a = f*E_t and b = 2(1-f)*E_t, where f is the fraction of flits followed directly by another. The measured b/a gives f = 0.59-0.61 on both meters and both sets. E_t would be about 163 fJ per bit-transition per hop, about 370 fF/mm: ordinary repeated-wire capacitance. Every one would then be two transitions, and b > a would not mean a one costs more than a transition.
- One constraint goes the other way. The frozen line sits on the model (-0.01 pJ/B/hop). If coupled wires dropped to zero between trains, and coupling also explained the 256 B shortfall (C6), the frozen line should sit about 0.11 pJ/B/hop above the model (estimate). So the data cannot pick the mechanism.
- Contention at d=4 adds mostly to the ones term: B rises by 222 from d=3 to 4, against 115-122 per step before. The idle-zero reading predicts the opposite, because busier links have fewer train ends.
- Precharged dynamic logic is unlikely in a synthesized NetSpeed NoC. The realistic precharged elements are buffer arrays with precharged read lines.
verdicts.required_change:
1. Retitle section 5 from 'A one costs more than a flip' to 'Ones cost energy, not just flips'. Relabel the KPI 'A one against a flip' as 'fitted cost per one-bit vs per flit-to-flit difference, loaded mesh', and add that these are fit coefficients, not a physical ranking.
2. Replace the mechanism paragraph with: 'A cost per one-bit that does not need the bit to differ from the previous flit needs wires or nodes that rest at 0. The simplest case is ordinary logic whose output goes to 0 when no flit is present, such as a crossbar with no grant or data gated by valid. Then each one rises and falls at the ends of a train of flits, and a and b are the same energy per transition, split by how often flits come back to back: about 60% here, which would put a transition near 160 fJ per hop, ordinary wire capacitance. Precharged structures, such as buffer arrays with precharged read lines, would also do it. The fit cannot tell these apart; slowing the flows at a fixed distance would.'
3. In the lede, write 'A stream of all ones, which never differs from one flit to the next, costs as much per hop as random data (5-9% more), though at one hop it costs about a third less in total.'
4. In section 3, say that 2P(1-P) is the difference rate between consecutive data flits, not necessarily the transition rate on the wires.

verdicts.claim: C3. Contention costs energy. With link-disjoint flows the NoC-rail data part is 90 fJ/bit/hop against 119 on the loaded set (up to 72% of link-hops shared), zeros 43 against 76; the two agree at d=1; board 107/186 and 56/103. The report says the extra is flits held in router buffers and arbitrated.
verdicts.evidence:
The numbers are reproduced by both independent analyses.

Sharing from the recorded target maps (XY routing) is 0/22/32/55% at d=1/2/3/4, and 72% only at d=6. wu has no d=5, and the body says 'at five or six'.

Per-reader bandwidth is almost the same in the two sets. wu against wsep at d=1-4: 45.7/46.7, 41.4/41.9, 37.3/38.0 and 32.8/34.8 GB/s, within 1-6%. Bandwidth falls with distance even on disjoint links, so it is latency-bound, and flits in wu are not held long. For unique random lines, interleaving flows cannot raise the difference rate between flits, so the extra data cost must be extra work per flit.

Sharing, not turns, looks like the driver at d=2-3. The straight x-only and y-only v1 flows, which share 0.8-2.1 link-hops per flow, cost +14-20% in the data part over wsep, similar to wu.

But sharing alone does not explain it:
- x-only at d=4 shares 56% of link-hops with the same mean link traffic as wu d=4 (about 55 GB/s), yet costs only +4% against wu's +19%. waxis at d=4 is anomalous in general.
- Within wu, regressing A and B on d plus shared link-hops per flow gives a sharing coefficient near 0, though d and sharing are collinear.
- wsep also differs in other ways: straight paths only (66-100% of wu flows turn), one reader per target (wu has up to 2), and 14-31 readers instead of 32.

At d=1 the sets agree within 3% for random data but differ by 5% for zeros on the NoC rail.
verdicts.required_change:
1. Replace 'up to 72% of link-hops at five or six' with '22-32% at two or three hops, 55% at four, 72% at six'.
2. Replace the mechanism sentence with: 'The difference is energy the loaded mesh spends beyond carrying the bits, most likely buffer writes and arbitration where flows meet. Per-reader bandwidth is within 6% of the link-disjoint set, so flits are not held long. The disjoint set also differs in having only straight paths, one reader per target and fewer readers.'
3. At d=1, say 'agree within 3% (5% for zeros on the mesh rail)'.
4. In the lede, replace 'as much as a third more distance' with '39% more on the mesh rail, 66% more on board power'.

verdicts.claim: C4. One hop = 3.72 mm (3.64-3.76), with x and y pitches 3.73/3.70 mm; x-only and y-only paths cost the same within 2% (125 and 128 fJ per random bit per hop).
verdicts.evidence:
pitch.json gives x/y pitches of 254.7 and 252.7 px, a ratio of 1.008 that is the same in all three copies of the die plot. Equal pitches predict equal x and y cost, so the test is a consistency check. It cannot split router from wire energy, which the report says.

A hop is one tile pitch of displacement for identical tiles. The routed wire can only be longer, so 'per mm' is an upper bound per mm of wire.

The y value rests on aifoundry3 alone, because aifoundry2's y/hop3 bursts are all dropped. It also needs 4 aifoundry3 bursts whose meter reads took 0.40-0.55 s. With those dropped, y is 112 against x 125, a 10% gap.
verdicts.required_change: Write: 'x-only and y-only paths cost the same within 2% over 1-3 hops on aifoundry3. y cannot be fitted on aifoundry2, and they are 10% apart if bursts with slow meter readings are dropped.' Add: 'per mm means per mm of displacement; the routed wire can only be longer.'

verdicts.claim: C5. Headline per random bit per mm at 0.485 V: 24+12 = 36 fJ uncontended on the NoC rail, 29+15 = 44 on board, loaded 31+20 = 50 and 46+27 = 73. Scaled by 3.44 to 0.9 V, the data part is 84-159, bracketing Dally's 100 and Keckler's 121. 'In capacitance per mm of mesh travel, routers included, the chip is where 40 nm wires were; its advantage is almost all V².' A bare 7 nm wire would be 12-24 fJ, 'a third to a half of what the mesh measures: the rest is the routers' flops, buffers and crossbar, and the extra paid for ones'.
verdicts.evidence:
The arithmetic reproduces: 24.3+11.6, 28.9+14.9, 30.6+19.8, 46.1+26.8, and (0.9/0.485)² = 3.4435. The interpretations overreach:

1. Board power should not be V²-scaled. It includes regulator loss, which is not switched capacitance on the die and shrinks as a fraction at higher output voltage. Scaling the NoC rail alone gives 84-105, which brackets 100 and sits below 121.
2. 'The voltage behind the lineage' is an inference; SYNTHESIS says no source states Dally's voltage. His 2023 slide puts about 0.5 V next to the figure. His own later figures, 20-40 fJ/b-mm (VLSI 2018) and about 30 (CACM 2022), match the unscaled 24-46.
3. Scaling the literature down is equivalent and cleaner. Keckler's 121 at 0.9 V becomes 35 fJ at 0.485 V, so the mesh (routers included) costs 0.69 of it uncontended and 0.87 loaded on the NoC rail.
4. 'Where 40 nm wires were' is expected, not a finding. Keckler assumes, and Dally 2018 states ('about 200fF/mm and independent of scaling'), that wire capacitance per mm hardly changes with process node.
5. The report's own estimates disagree with each other. The first-principles wire model at 0.9 V gives 41-81 (report.json first_principles.at_09), half of Keckler's 121. So 'where 40 nm wires were' and 'a bare 7 nm wire is 1/3-1/2 of the mesh' use references a factor of 2 apart.
6. The uncontended NoC data part (24) sits at the top of the bare-wire range (12-24). Loaded it is 31, 1.3-2.6x the range; board is 1.2-3.9x. So the 'rest is routers' conclusion does not follow. Rough estimate: a router's per-bit data path (a few flops, a 5-8-input mux, maybe a buffer write) is tens of fF, against about 1 pF for 3.7 mm of wire. A large router share is physically unlikely unless flits are written to SRAM buffers.
7. The per-random-bit capacitance assumes 0.5 transitions per bit per hop. In the idle-zero reading of C2, random data make about 0.7, and the capacitance per transition is about 370 fF/mm (loaded NoC rail) instead of 520.
verdicts.required_change:
1. Lede: 'Scaled to 0.9 V, the voltage of Keckler 2011's 40 nm figure from which Dally's number most likely descends (no source states Dally's voltage), the mesh-rail data-dependent cost is 84-105 fJ per bit·mm.' Scale only the mesh rail, and change KPI k-09 accordingly.
2. Section 8: 'At equal voltage, the mesh's data-dependent energy per random bit per mm of travel, routers included, is 0.7-0.9 of Keckler's 40 nm repeated-wire figure (35 fJ at 0.485 V) on the mesh rail. Wire capacitance per mm barely changes between nodes, so this is what one expects if most of a hop's data-dependent energy is its 3.7 mm of wire. The mesh is cheaper than the 0.9 V literature because it runs at 0.485 V. Dally's own 16 nm figure of 20-40 fJ/b·mm matches it without any scaling.'
3. Replace the first-principles sentence with: 'A plain repeated wire, estimated from a predictive 7 nm kit (ASAP7) with Ho's repeater factors, would cost about 12-24 fJ per random bit·mm at 0.485 V (41-81 at 0.9 V, half of Keckler's figure). The uncontended mesh-rail data cost, 24, is at the top of that range; the data do not show how much the routers add.'
4. Delete 'this 7 nm chip is where 40 nm wires were; its advantage is almost all V²' and 'the rest is the routers' flops, buffers and crossbar'.

verdicts.claim: C6. Blocks of 16-128 B cost the same per hop and 256 B blocks about 0.8 pJ/B/hop more on board power. This is explained by 4 mesh lanes chosen by PA[7:6] (on one lane consecutive lines are i and i+4) and by a flit of at least 64 B. The 256 B case is about 60% of the full-flip prediction because other loads and flows slip in between.
verdicts.evidence:
The lane mechanism is supported by the sources:
- In the clean-room shirecache_mesh_master.sv, the port for a remote scratchpad access is scp_bank_id = address[BankLsb=6 +: 2], i.e. PA[7:6].
- The spec routes SCP requests to banks by PA[7:6] and gives 4 to_l3 mesh ports.
- etsoc_shire_other_esr.h lists 4 to_l3 master and 4 L3 slave NoC bridges per shire (l2tol3/b/c/d and l3/b/c/d), with 9 routers per stop.
- That each lane is its own physical channel end to end is plausible but not shown.

The lane model predicts no excess for N ≤ 128 and full flips for N = 256, which matches the pattern. Measured values: 1.195-1.209 pJ/B at d=1 for N ≤ 128, and the model's t=0 prediction is within 1% at d=1, 3 and 6.

The shortfall explanation is contradicted (perd_v1.py):
- On the NoC rail the 256 B excess is 0.52/0.48/0.53 of the per-distance full-flip prediction at d=1/3/6, and 0.54 per hop. That includes d=1, where no link is shared. Board gives about 0.66.
- Other flows cannot explain a constant fraction at d=1.
- The other in-flight load is ruled out by v1: its two in-flight loads carry identical lines, yet its transition coefficient equals v2's (A(1) 297-301 vs 299-304).
- A physical candidate is that when every wire flips the same way at once, the coupling capacitance between neighbours is not charged, so a full flip costs about C_ground/(C_ground+2C_coupling) of a random-data transition. Packing of lines into wider flits is another. The data do not settle it.

Most of the 256 B excess is at the shire crossing: 1.26 pJ/B at d=1 against 0.41 per further hop.

The flit-width argument is slightly loose. With 32 B flits the 16 B pattern gives two identical halves; only the 32 B pattern would flip.
verdicts.required_change: Replace the last two sentences of section 7 with: 'The 256-byte pattern costs about half (mesh rail) to two thirds (board) of what the model predicts if every bit flipped on every flit, at every distance including one hop, where no link is shared. So it is not other flows slipping in, and v1's identical in-flight loads show it is not the other load either. One possible cause: when all wires flip the same way together, the capacitance between neighbours is not charged. Most of the excess is paid at the shire crossing.' Also write: 'if flits were 32 B the 32 B pattern would flip; if 16 B, the 16 B pattern.'

verdicts.claim: C7. A random byte costs 1.5-2.2 pJ per hop. A 64 B line across 10 hops costs 1.0-1.4 nJ against 7.8 nJ from DRAM, so it is 6-8x cheaper. A 32-bit operand crossing one hop costs about 6-9 pJ, about one lane of fadd.ps (5.3 pJ).
verdicts.evidence:
The arithmetic holds:
- 187.6 and 274 fJ/bit/hop give 1.50 and 2.19 pJ/B.
- 64 × 15.0 to 22.0 pJ/B gives 0.97 to 1.41 nJ.
- DRAM is 122 pJ/B × 64 = 7.8 nJ.
- 32 × 50.4 × 3.72 = 6.0 pJ and 32 × 72.9 × 3.72 = 8.7 pJ; 42.2 / 8 = 5.3 pJ.

The DRAM comparison is not like for like. The DRAM figure is board power for a whole load, endpoints included. The hand-off figure counts hops only, and at one end uses the mesh rail. A straight-line fit to v2 wu random on board power (leakage-corrected) gives an intercept of 6.61 and a slope of 2.17 pJ/B. At 10 hops that is 28.3 pJ/B = 1.81 nJ per line, 4.3x cheaper than DRAM. The mesh-rail 1.0 nJ should not be compared with a board-level DRAM figure.

Comparing board to board, one hop costs 8.7/5.3 = 1.6 fp32 adds, so 'roughly a hop' holds to within 2x.
verdicts.required_change: Write: 'Including the reads, writes and shire crossings at either end, a random 64-byte line handed 10 hops away costs about 1.8 nJ of board power, 4-5x less than reading it from DRAM (7.8 nJ). The hops alone cost 1.4 nJ.' Say the fadd comparison is board to board: one hop costs about 1-1.6 lanes of fadd.ps.

verdicts.claim: C8. Some traffic (s to s+16 rings; on aifoundry2 the y-only pairs 3 hops apart) starves the service processor's management path, so reads take 0.8-1.6 s and the bursts are dropped; a sampler killed mid-request poisons the management queue.
verdicts.evidence:
The aifoundry2 part is in the data. wire.json drops the 6 aifoundry2 waxis/y/hop3 bursts, and the independent analyses find reads of 0.8-1.62 s there. The pipeline records the reason as 'too few samples'.

aifoundry3 showed milder slowing on the same traffic (0.40-0.55 s) and those bursts were kept, and they carry the C4 y value.

No s to s+16 ring bursts, and no evidence of management-queue poisoning, are in these four data sets or in wire.json, so those parts cannot be checked here. That the slowdown comes through the service processor's management path over the mesh is an inference, not measured.
verdicts.required_change: Write: 'on aifoundry2 the y-only pairs 3 hops apart (0.8-1.6 s per reading; those bursts are dropped; aifoundry3 slowed to 0.4-0.55 s on the same traffic and was kept)'. Either cite the report or run where the rings and queue poisoning were seen, or drop them from this report.

verdicts.claim: Interpretation: a per-one cost is the signature of return-to-zero or precharged (dynamic) circuits, and 'a carried 1 costs more than a transition' (KPI k-one, section 5 title).
verdicts.evidence:
The ones term needs something that rests at 0. The simplest candidate, static logic that outputs 0 when idle, makes a and b the same per-transition energy split by occupancy: f = 2a/(2a+b) = 0.59-0.61, E_t about 163 fJ per hop, about 370 fF/mm. In that case 'a one costs more than a flip' is a feature of how the fit is written, not of the circuit.

Dynamic logic is implausible in a synthesized NetSpeed NoC. Precharged buffer read lines are possible.

The frozen line fitting while the 256 B pattern reaches only half the predicted flip cost argues against 'coupled wires drop to zero between trains' as the whole story. So the mechanism is open; the report's hedge 'the fit cannot say which circuit' is right, but the headline wording is not.
verdicts.required_change: Keep 'the fit cannot say which circuit it is'. Name the ordinary idle-to-zero mechanism first, with what it implies for a and b. Remove every statement that a one physically costs more than a transition (section 5 title, KPI sub-label, the lede's 'every one carried').

verdicts.claim: Interpretation: the bus-inversion suggestion (send the complement plus a flag when more than half the bits are ones; an all-ones stream would travel almost free).
verdicts.evidence:
The model is symmetric in transitions and asymmetric in P, so ones-minimising inversion does lower the ones term for dense data. But:
- All-ones becomes all-zeros, which still pays the data-independent part: 73.8 of 203 fJ/bit/hop on the loaded NoC rail, 36% of its current cost. That is not 'almost free'.
- For random data, per-flit inversion of 512 bits lowers the ones density only from 0.5 to 0.482, saving about 2.3 of 188 fJ/bit/hop (1.2%).
- Per-byte inversion reaches a density of 0.363 but adds a flag wire for every 8 data wires, leaving a net saving of a few percent.
- The NoC here is fixed hardware. The only option on this chip is choosing a representation in software, such as storing ones-dense data complemented.
- If the ones term is idle-to-zero, holding the last value on idle cycles would remove it entirely, which is a better lesson for designers.
verdicts.required_change: Write: 'For data dense in ones, storing or sending the complement would make it cost what its complement costs. All-ones data would then cost what zeros cost, still the data-independent ~40% of a random bit's per-hop cost. For random data the saving is about 1%. On this chip only software can choose the representation.' Drop 'would travel almost free'.

verdicts.claim: Interpretation: 'per mm of mesh travel' is comparable with Dally's per-mm figure.
verdicts.evidence: Dally uses 100 fJ/b-mm for distances travelled between blocks (the 2023 slide on a 48 mm GPU-die round trip; CACM 2020 'communication between blocks on chip'). So per mm of mesh travel, routers included, matches how he uses it. Keckler's 310 pJ for 256 bits over 10 mm is a bare repeated wire, so the mesh figure is an upper bound when compared with it. The report already says 'a bare wire costs less'.
verdicts.required_change: Say explicitly in section 8 that Keckler's figure is a bare repeated wire, so the mesh figure is an upper bound against it, and that per mm means per mm of displacement.

other_issues: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/lit/first-principles-estimate.md is not the estimate. It is OpenROAD's parasitics-estimation manual (set_wire_rc and similar). The actual arithmetic is only in lit/wire_calc.py and SYNTHESIS.md section 1f. Fix or remove the file before the report points readers at the research folder.

SYNTHESIS.md's bottom line and conversion tables use the older E27 data: d=8, q=0.445, 35/26 fJ, 101-137 fJ at 0.9 V. They differ from this report's numbers. Because the report cites SYNTHESIS for sources, add a note that its measured numbers are superseded by this experiment.

The report's own reference points disagree by 2x. The first-principles repeated wire at 0.9 V (41-81 fJ per random bit·mm, report.json first_principles.at_09) is half of Keckler's 121. So Keckler's figure contains more than an ideal repeated wire, or uses a different transition convention. Say so wherever both are used.

A test that would separate the explanations for the 256 B shortfall: alternate 256 B blocks of 0x55 and 0xAA instead of 0x00 and 0xFF. Every wire still flips, but neighbours flip in opposite directions, so the coupling capacitance is charged at double weight. If coupling explains the shortfall, 0x55/0xAA should cost well above the random-data prediction; if packing or ordering does, both patterns should cost the same. Throttling the flows at a fixed distance would separate the idle-to-zero and precharge readings of the ones term.

The loaded-mesh fixed and data parts rest on bandwidth that falls with distance equally on disjoint links (46.7 down to 32.1 GB/s per reader for wsep at d=1-5). So the 'per second rather than per hop' caveat applies to the uncontended numbers too, not only the loaded ones.

Section 5 and the KPI mix loaded and uncontended numbers without saying so. The per-one and per-transition values (35 and 26 fJ/mm) come only from the loaded all-pairs set; wsep ran only P = 0 and 0.5, so those terms cannot be separated without contention. Label them 'loaded mesh'.

At near-threshold 0.485 V, FinFET gate capacitance is somewhat lower than at 0.9 V. So even for full-swing links, V² scaling at constant capacitance slightly understates the 0.9 V figure. If the links are low-swing, it overstates it (energy goes as Vdd×Vswing). Keep the existing caveat and note both directions.

verdicts.lens: ARITHMETIC, UNITS AND SOURCES. I built the page with scripts/build-report.py into verify-hpm/arith/page.html. A node DOM shim (verify-hpm/arith/render.js) ran the page's own script and printed every number the text shows. verify-hpm/arith/check.py then recomputed each conversion from report.json and wire.json: pJ/B/hop x125 = fJ/bit/hop, divided by 3.72 = fJ/bit/mm, the 0.5a+0.5b random bit, the pitch folding, the V^2 factor, and the C7 ratios. I checked the literature numbers against the local copies of the original PDFs in scratchpad/wire-research/lit (Keckler 2011 Table 1, Dally AHA 2023, CACM 2020, CACM 2022, VLSI 2018, Yale Patt 75, Ho 2003), and the geometry against research/geometry/pitch.json. Every printed number follows from wire.json with the correct unit conversions. What fails are several sentences whose wording does not match the numbers next to them: a false "brackets", "a third more", "72% at five or six", "within 2%", and a DRAM ratio that mixes meters.

verdicts.claim: C1. Energy per byte grows linearly with d for every pattern; on the NoC rail the data part is ~0 at d=0 and grows by a constant per hop; leaving the shire costs about one extra hop.
verdicts.evidence: Data part at d=0, from wire.json configs (wu, NoC): p0.5 hop0 0.035 minus p0 hop0 0.012 = 0.023 pJ/B, against 1.55 at d=1. So ~0 holds. Per-hop steps of the data part (random minus zeros) are 0.89, 0.90, 1.09 and 0.79 pJ/B/hop, roughly constant (+-13%). The exit cost, (line intercept - d0)/slope with the line fitted over d=1-6: board, wu P=0.5: 1.12 hops. NoC rail, wu: P=0.5 0.55, zeros 0.29, P=1 -0.09 hops. Link-disjoint wsep on NoC: random 1.15, zeros 1.32. Section 4 puts 'Leaving the shire costs about one hop more' straight after 'On the mesh rail ...' and under a chart of the loaded wu sweep. On that meter and that sweep the exit cost is 0.55 hop for random data and zero for all-ones. Both independent re-analyses agree (0.53-0.74 NoC loaded, 1.05-1.18 board).
verdicts.required_change: Section 4: replace 'Leaving the shire costs about one hop more (the mesh-stop crossings)' with: 'Leaving the shire costs about one more hop on board power, and for link-disjoint flows on the mesh rail; in this loaded sweep the mesh rail shows about half a hop for random data and none for all-ones.' verdicts.claim: C2. Per-hop energy depends on the density of ones; model s0 + a*2P(1-P) + b*P; v2 NoC a=98, b=129, board 151/192; v1 NoC 95/131, board 139/197; rms 0.008 (NoC) and ~0.04 (board); complement tests 132 and 129.
verdicts.evidence: The wire.json model gives: v2 NoC a 98.1, b 129.4; v2 board 151.0/192.0; v1 NoC 95.3/131.3; v1 board 138.5/196.6 fJ. rms 0.0084 and 0.0382 (v2), 0.0084 and 0.0397 (v1) pJ/B/hop. complement_test gives 131.8 (3/4 vs 1/4) and 128.8 (1 vs 0) fJ. The conversion is right: the coefficient in pJ/B/hop per unit t or P is divided by 8 and multiplied by 1000, which gives fJ per bit-transition (or per one-bit) per hop. The random bit is 0.5a+0.5b = 113.8 NoC and 171.5 board. The per-mm table values (26.4, 34.8, 30.6, 19.8, total 50.4 NoC; 40.6, 51.6, 46.1, 26.8, total 72.9 board) are these divided by 3.72. Their brackets are lo/3.76 and hi/3.64, as the caption says. Both independent re-analyses reproduce the NoC numbers within 1-3%. The board a moves by 7-16% with the leakage treatment (independent methods), but that is outside this lens. All-ones costs 5-9% more per hop than random (NoC P=1 1.629 against P=0.5 1.500 pJ/B/hop), so 'about as much' is fair.

verdicts.claim: C3. Contention costs energy: wsep (d=1-5) NoC data 90 (90.6/90.1) against wu (d=1-4, up to 72% of link-hops shared) 119; zeros 43 against 76; board 107 against 186, and 56 against 103; at d=1 they agree.
verdicts.evidence: The numbers match wire.json disjoint_flows. NoC: wsep 90.4 (90.6/90.1), zeros 43.1; wu 119.2 and 76.4. Board: wsep 107.4 and 55.5; wu 186.0 and 103.0. Three problems. The all-pairs sweep has no d=5 (configs hop0,1,2,3,4,6), so the body's 'up to 72% of link-hops at five or six' is wrong on both counts. The free-link board per-mm data figure therefore moves from 28.9 to 32.7. (3) The lede says 'contention costs as much as a third more distance'. The numbers beside it are 36 to 50 fJ/mm (+41%) and 44 to 73 (+67%). The like-for-like C3 totals are wu/wsep 1.47 (NoC) and 1.77 (board). None of these is 'a third'.
verdicts.required_change: Section 6: replace '(none at one hop, up to 72% of link-hops at five or six)' with '(none at one hop, 22-32% at two and three, 55% at four, 72% at six)'. verdicts.claim: C7. A random byte costs 1.5-2.2 pJ/hop; a 64 B line across 10 hops (~37 mm) costs 1.0-1.4 nJ against 7.8 nJ from DRAM, so the farthest on-chip hand-off is 6-8x cheaper; a 32-bit operand crossing one hop costs ~6-9 pJ, about one lane of fadd.ps (5.3 pJ); an fp add is worth roughly a hop.

DRAM 64x121.96 = 7.81 nJ (manual.json reruns.levels dram). The ratios are 5.62-8.13, printed as 6-8. 10 x 3.72 = 37.2 mm, and 10 is the Manhattan diameter of the 6x6 minion grid, the same convention as Dally's '40mm corner to corner'. fadd.ps: 42.20/8 = 5.27 pJ; 32 bits x one hop = 6.00-8.68 pJ. Problems: (1) The 8x end divides a board-power DRAM figure by a mesh-rail-only hop cost. Board against board, it is 5.6x. (2) The DRAM figure is a whole read. The observability report says it includes 50-60 pJ/B of mesh, SRAM and delivery. The hop figure leaves out the far scratchpad read and the exit. Counting them, from the wu P=0.5 board line (intercept 6.79 + 10x2.18 = 28.6 pJ/B; d=0 is 4.34), gives 4.3x. (3) The operand and add comparisons also mix meters. Board against board, one hop is 1.65 fadd lanes, so a lane is worth about 0.6 hop (~2.3 mm). Dally's CACM 2022 accounting counts both 32-bit operands (1.9 pJ per mm for two words), which would halve it again. (4) 'a third to a half' of the 4.21 pJ own-scratchpad read uses the rail number for the low end; board against board it is 0.52. (5) The 10 hops are extrapolated beyond the measured d <= 6, and on the loaded mesh the per-hop increment grows with d.
